Article Title: Singapore burns its garbage and dumps the ash into the sea; how a 350-hectare island became a wildlife haven
Article Text:
Burn first, then bank

Eventually, grass and plants grow on the surface of the landfill, transforming it into a green expanse.

A growing land

Visitors walk the reef flats at low tide, spotting starfish, octopus and living coral, on an island made of incinerated garbage.

Did you know Singapore has a trash island made from ash? The country has managed to create a 350-hectare land area that has transformed into an ecological haven where migratory birds reside and corals thrive. The idea stems from a problem unique to the nation, it does not have much land to spare.A city-state located on an island smaller than New York City, housing a population of six million cannot lease land for dumping. So what does it do? It builds its landfills in the sea and turns them into exemplary nature reserves. Semakau Landfill, eight kilometres off the main island is the world's first landfill created entirely in ocean space. It also stands as one of the most peculiar stories of successful waste management, being the only landfill in the country. It contributes to making Singapore well known around the world as a clean city-state. The landfill is designed, constructed and managed by the National Environment Agency of Singapore (NEA).The system begins with burning waste. Singapore incinerates the overwhelming majority of its solid waste at waste-to-energy plants which do two jobs at once: generate electricity and shrink the garbage by up to 90%.What is left after this is ash and other material that cannot be burned. That leftover, roughly a couple of thousand tonnes a day, is what goes to sea. Barges carry the incineration ash and non-burnable waste out to Semakau each night, where it is tipped into engineered cells and capped. Eventually, grass and plants grow on the surface of the landfill, transforming it into a green expanse.This is also where engineering comes into play. Rather than piling fill on existing land, planners enclosed 350 hectares of sea between two small islands, Pulau Semakau and Pulau Sakeng, inside a seven-kilometre perimeter rock bund, a rock wall drawn around a patch of ocean. The bund was lined with an impermeable membrane and a layer of marine clay, sealing the enclosed water off from the strait so that leachate, the toxic liquid that drains from any landfill, stays inside and gets treated on site rather than leaking into the sea. Cells within the ring are pumped dry and filled with ash. Opened on April 1, 1999, Semakau became Singapore’s only landfill, and is expected to keep taking the country’s ash until 2035.What makes Semakau famous is that the marine life has survived not only around it, but also in it. While 13 hectares of mangrove were destroyed to raise the bund, ecologists and biologists were brought in to replant the mangroves at the disturbed sites as compensation. Around the landfill’s western shores, the original seagrass meadows, coral reefs and remaining mangroves were protected through construction and largely came through intact. The result is a landfill fringed by functioning ecosystems: reefs, seagrass and mangroves rich enough that the intertidal flats host creatures now rarely seen on Singapore’s developed mainland.In 2005, the government transformed the landfill into a recreation site. Now, people can take guided intertidal walks, birdwatching, sport fishing and stargazing. Visitors walk the reef flats at low tide, spotting starfish, octopus and living coral, on an island made of incinerated garbage.While Semakau provides a solution for Singapore's waste, it is not a permanent one. In the end, it is a landfill that is filling up. Now, the country is researching ways to recycle incineration ash into construction material as the next step forward.

Article Title: Built in 1878, this 8,500-sq-ft Ohio jail held prisoners for 110 years; 148 years later, a developer bought it and may turn its cells into offices or a speakeasy
Article Text:
Built in 1878 by Toledo architect David Gibbs, the building operated as a working jail until 1988. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1990.

A jail with more than 100 years of history

From prison cells to private offices

A speakeasy behind bars?

Preserving the past while moving forward

A former Ohio jail that spent more than a century behind bars is getting a very different future. The historic Jail and Sheriff’s Residence in Delaware, Ohio, has been sold by the Delaware County Historical Society to Westwood principal Andy Warnock, a Delaware native, states the Columbus Business First report. The 8,500-square-foot property, which once housed prisoners and the county sheriff’s family, is now being repositioned as a mixed-use property that could include private offices, creative space and an unusual nod to its Prohibition-era past. The sale follows more than five years of stewardship by the Historical Society, which purchased the building in 2021 and worked to make it accessible through tours, exhibitions and community events, adds the report.Built in 1878 by Toledo architect David Gibbs, the building operated as a working jail until 1988. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1990. Its architecture is primarily Italianate, with Gothic Revival and Second Empire influences that reflect the period in which it was built. The property also offers a glimpse into changing attitudes toward incarceration in 19th-century Ohio. The jail contains 18 cells, with 16 originally intended for men and two for women.The sheriff lived on the premises with his family, while the sheriff’s wife, known as the Matron, had responsibilities that included preparing meals and caring for inmates. The arrangement was part of a broader prison-reform movement associated with Ohio Governor Rutherford B. Hayes, who was born and raised in Delaware.The new plans are considerably more modern. Renovations to the property include HVAC and electrical improvements, along with updates to the rooms in the former residential section. Eight private offices are planned for that portion of the building, while shared amenities will include a kitchenette, conference room and lounge.Westwood Real Estate Co., the brokerage arm of Westwood Collective, plans to use part of the renovated space as it expands into the Delaware market and recruits residential and commercial real estate agents. Architects Dave Kerr and Cara Hering of DK Architects are working on the project.Perhaps the most intriguing possibility involves the jail itself. The existing cells are expected to receive their own refresh during a second phase of renovation. Among the concepts being considered for the rear portion of the building are a Prohibition-era speakeasy and a maker’s space combined with an art gallery. It is a fittingly unconventional next act for a building that has already served as a jail, residence, museum and even wedding venue. In October 2025, the property hosted nine weddings during a Halloween-themed event organized by the City of Delaware and the Historical Society. Court employees dressed in costume while the entrance and cells were decorated for the occasion.For Warnock, the project represents more than another real estate investment. As a Delaware native, he is bringing two decades of industry experience back to his hometown while taking on the challenge of giving one of its most recognizable buildings a useful new life. The goal now is to preserve the character that makes the old jail special while allowing the property to function in a very different era. If the plans come together, the building's cells may soon hold businesses, artists or late-night patrons rather than prisoners, an unusual transformation for a landmark that has witnessed nearly 150 years of Delaware history.Image Courtesy: istock and Columbus Business First
Article Summary: The historic Jail and Sheriff’s Residence in Delaware, Ohio, has been sold by the Delaware County Historical Society. The 8,500-square-foot property is now being repositioned as a mixed-use property that could include private offices, creative space and an unusual nod to its Prohibition-era past. Built in 1878 by Toledo architect David Gibbs, the building operated as a working jail until 1988.

Article Title: ​In 2002, a collector bought a 75-cent record at a New York flea market; it turned out to be one of only two surviving Velvet Underground acetates and sold for $25,200
Article Text:
A rare recording on acetate

Finding it in a flea market

During a stroll through the Chelsea fire sales, a collector got his hands on something one can only dream about. And yet, that was exactly what happened to Warren Hill in 2002. He picked up an acetate record at a flea market in New York for the price of a coffee. He bought one of only two surviving copies of The Velvet Underground's secret tape session. He eventually sold it for $25,200!He didn’t have a collector’s savvy eye. It was rather plain luck that landed him a piece of music history. When he bought the record alongside damaged LPs from estate sales and fire-damaged lots, he didn’t expect he was going to make a fortune out of it. He had no idea that the 1966 recording, known as the ‘Scepter Studios’ acetate, contained nine early versions of songs that would later appear on The Velvet Underground & Nico, the band’s influential 1967 debut album. Four years after finding it, Hill sold the acetate for $25,200, Rolling Stone reported.The acetate was created in April 1966, before The Velvet Underground had signed with a record label. Andy Warhol had already established himself as the band's manager. He knew The Velvet Underground's music was unlikely to appeal to major labels, so he planned a secret recording session.Engineer Norman Dolph recorded the band at Scepter Studios after hours.He was reportedly paid with a painting from Warhol for making the recording. Warhol took the acetate directly to the gatekeepers. Columbia said no. Atlantic said no. Elektra politely declined. It took Verve Records to finally agree to distribute the band's debut, which hit shelves in 1967 under the iconic banana sticker design.The Scepter recording remained buried, known only to those who had handled it in person. Warhol wanted to make the recording before the band signed to a label so record companies could not interfere with its music. After recording, Dolph sent the acetate to Columbia Records, Atlantic and Elektra. All of them said no. Verve Records eventually agreed to distribute the band's debut album. So, for years, the Scepter recording remained buried, and nobody knew about it other than the team. Only two original copies of the acetate are known to survive. The other is owned by Velvet Underground drummer Maureen Tucker.These acetates mean a lot in the music industry, though longevity is not their strongest suit. The material is unstable, so most collectors know that twenty to thirty spins can destroy the record. But, to everyone’s surprise, this particular disc somehow survived fire damage, decades of storage and the general degradation that time inflicts.In 2002, record collector Warren Hill came across it at a street sale in New York City. The acetate record only cost him 75 cents. Four years later, he listed it on eBay and watched the bidding price climb past $150,000. But then the buyer backed out. He put the acetate up for auction again, this time with stricter requirements for potential buyers. The sale eventually settled at $25,200 with legitimate verification.The anonymous collector who bought it then chose a path most wouldn't. He locked the acetate away and never played it. Not once. He knew how fragile the record was. He wasn’t ready to take any risks. “It wasn’t worth it to me to even handle the record, let alone drag a needle across it. This is not a conventional record that can be played thousands and thousands of times. It’s an acetate; it’s the equivalent of a CD you’d burn 10 years ago,” he told Rolling Stone. He treated it as a financial stake in music history. And he was indeed right to.In 2012, when the 45th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition of The Velvet Underground & Nico arrived, it included a remastered version of these sessions on the fourth disc, pulled from Maureen Tucker's identical copy, the only other acetate known to exist. Record stores sold 5,000 limited copies during Record Store Day. Suddenly, millions could hear what Warhol had hidden. And the other copy was auctioned again, this time for even more.
Article Summary: The acetate was created in April 1966, before The Velvet Underground had signed with a record label. Andy Warhol wanted to make the recording before the band signed to a label so record companies could not interfere with its music. The recording remained buried, known only to those who had handled it in person. In 2002, record collector Warren Hill came across it at a street sale in New York City. The acetate record only cost him 75 cents. Four years later, Hill sold the acetate for $25,200.

Article Title: In 1966, a New York art teacher paid under $100 for a thrift-store painting; 60 years later the FCB Cadell work sold for £189,200
Article Text:
The painting depicts Cadell's north-facing studio on the first floor of his home in Edinburgh

How the painting was identified

The artist behind the work

What “The Lady in Black” shows

A painting from Cadell's peak period

In 1966, retired art teacher Helene Plotkin bought a painting for less than $100 at a thrift store in White Plains, New York. She liked the work enough to take it home and display it, but she had no idea that the painting was by a well-known Scottish artist.According to People's magazine, Plotkin kept the painting in her home for nearly 60 years. It was only in 2025, when her son Barry began researching it and took it for appraisal, that the family learnt more about its origins. The work was eventually identified as a painting by Scottish artist Francis Campbell Boileau Cadell, commonly known as FCB Cadell.The painting, titled “Interior: The Lady in Black”, was later offered at auction by Edinburgh-based Lyon & Turnbull. It sold for £189,200, including the buyer's premium, in June 2026. The sale turned a painting bought for less than $100 decades ago into a highly valued work of art.For Plotkin, the discovery also confirmed something she had felt when she first saw the painting. She told the BBC that her background in art history and studio practice drew her to it immediately. “The painting had an undeniable, regal presence, but it was the color theory at play that held my attention,” she said.The painting's artist had remained unknown for years because its signature was difficult to read. That changed when Plotkin's son began looking into the work in 2025.The signature was deciphered with the help of artificial intelligence. Specialists at Lyon & Turnbull then examined the painting and confirmed that it was the work of Cadell.The discovery came after the painting had spent decades in the Plotkin family home. Her son said the family was surprised when they learnt who had created it and who was shown in the painting.“We were, as you can imagine, delighted and astounded when we found out the identity of the artist and of the model,” he said.“For mom, it was confirmation of her artistic eye and ability to recognize great talent,” he added.Cadell was one of four artists known as the Scottish Colourists. The group also included John Duncan Fergusson, George Leslie Hunter and Samuel John Peploe.According to Lyon & Turnbull, the four artists were influenced by developments in progressive French art during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They were known for their use of bright colours and expressive brushwork.The group exhibited together in London and Paris during the 1920s and 1930s. Lyon & Turnbull describes the Scottish Colourists as important figures in Scottish modern art and in British and European art history of the period.Cadell was particularly known for paintings of Edinburgh interiors and still-life works. “Interior: The Lady in Black” dates from what Lyon & Turnbull described as the most important and successful period of his career.The painting depicts Cadell's north-facing studio on the first floor of his home in Edinburgh. The room looks towards Fife and includes several details associated with the artist's interiors.Lyon & Turnbull said the work brings together several of Cadell's well-known objects and visual motifs. These include lilac walls, a highly polished black floor, mirrors, a Louis XV-style armchair, a blue and white coffee set and a black fan tied with ribbon.At the centre of the composition is the model May Easter. She was one of Cadell's most important sitters, alongside Bethia Hamilton Don Wauchope.Easter is shown seated on a bright red chair. Her red hair, golden turban and veil are among the details highlighted by Lyon & Turnbull in its description of the work.Cadell's use of black is also a noticeable feature of the painting. Easter's black clothing is contrasted with other colours and details in the room, including a pink rose at the base of her neckline.Lyon & Turnbull said the painting was created at the height of Cadell's career and described it as a “tour de force” example of his work.The artist had made a name for himself through solo exhibitions in London and Edinburgh before the First World War. After being demobilised from the army in 1919, he bought 6 Ainslie Place in Edinburgh's Georgian New Town the following year.The house became an important part of Cadell's work. He lived there until 1931, and its interiors became the subject of a series of paintings during the 1920s.
Article Summary: The painting, titled “Interior: The Lady in Black”, was later offered at auction by Edinburgh-based Lyon & Turnbull. It sold for £189,200, including the buyer's premium, in June 2026. It depicts Cadell's north-facing studio on the first floor of his home in Edinburgh.

Article Title: Australia switched on a $7.8 million wastewater plant that can process 700 megalitres a year; its inventor says it breaks down stubborn pollutants 16 times more efficiently
Article Text:
Being used in Dubbo

An average Australian household generates about 350 litres of wastewater daily. Combined across the country, this leads to hundreds of gigalitres of wastewater that is managed in the country by more than 720 sewage treatment plants. While the country turns a major portion of this water into recycled water for agriculture, industry and other fields, it takes immense energy and time for the process to complete.Now, the country has built a new method of recycling wastewater which uses less energy and works faster than conventional systems. Inventor Troy Warry said his system is about 16 times more efficient at breaking down stubborn pollutants in wastewater than conventional methods. The water treatment scientist explained that it was the product of years of "trial, error and sleepless nights and crying in the shower" for an end result that uses fewer chemicals and processes wastewater faster."There are a lot of advanced oxidation [systems] out there, but this is the first titanium dioxide-based one in the world where the catalyst is permanently immobilised inside the reactor while still remaining highly photoactive," he said to ABC News."It uses a lot less energy, produces much cleaner water, destroys contaminants in a lot shorter time frame, and sustains high flow rates every day for long periods."A key highlight for Warry is that rather than filtering out, the reactor destroys contaminants such as pesticides, petroleum hydrocarbons, pharmaceutical residues, antibiotics, hormones and other persistent organic compounds. "Instead of simply capturing those contaminants and creating another concentrated waste stream, the process attacks their chemical structure and tears the molecules apart," he said."By accelerating the reaction kinetics, we can destroy difficult contaminants much faster than traditional advanced oxidation, which can substantially reduce energy consumption while producing a much higher-quality treated water," he added.The new technology was developed and scaled through trial runs by Warry in Germany, Spain and Norway. It has now been built in Central NSW as part of a new $7.8 million advanced wastewater treatment plant (AWTP), which Dubbo Regional Council switched on this week.Squadron Energy contributed $3.6 million under an agreement that allows it to draw on the recycled water to build its three wind farms and a firming station in the Dubbo region. Rob Wheals, Squadron CEO, said the company's investment was an effort to reduce demand on local water resources so "drinking water is available for drinking," while leaving it as a legacy to benefit the community hosting its wind farms.Dubbo mayor Josh Black said the arrangement had helped shore up water security in the region. "[It] means we won't have to choose between drought and development," Mr Black said.As for Warry, he said he was not surprised that a regional council was the first to use the technology in Australia. "They have a vision that they want to provide better water security," he said. "Australia is going to have to reuse increasingly difficult water sources as populations grow, rainfall becomes less predictable and pressure on our existing supplies increases. It's ridiculous to think that all of the wastewater sitting in those lagoons is just getting wasted," he added.
Article Summary: An average Australian household generates about 350 litres of wastewater daily. Hundreds of gigalitres of wastewater is managed in the country by more than 720 sewage treatment plants. A new method of recycling wastewater uses less energy and works faster than conventional systems. It has been built in Central NSW as part of a new $7.8 million advanced wastewater treatment plant.

Article Title: Scientists built a wood-based sponge that pulls water from air as dry as 15% humidity; it produced up to 1.72 litres per kg per day
Article Text:
Image: AI-generated representation of a wood-based sponge that pulls water from air as dry as 15% humidity

Wood sponge captures moisture from air at 15% humidity

Researchers combined the wood sponge with a solar heat store

The wood-based system produced up to 1.72 litres of water per kg

Northeast Forestry University researchers designed the sponge for all-weather water harvesting

Water vapour is present almost everywhere, even in places where rivers, lakes and groundwater are scarce. The challenge has always been turning that invisible moisture into usable freshwater efficiently enough to make atmospheric water harvesting practical. Now, researchers have developed a wood-based material that can capture water from remarkably dry air. The sponge continued absorbing moisture at relative humidity as low as 15%, while a larger system built from the material produced as much as 1.72 litres of freshwater per kilogram of sorbent per day during outdoor testing.The technology combines a porous sponge made from balsa wood with lithium chloride, a moisture-attracting salt, and a separate layer designed to capture and store solar heat. This allows the material to absorb water vapour from the atmosphere and then release the collected water even when sunlight becomes weak or disappears.The work, published in Nature Communications under the title ‘ Hygroscopic wood sponge with dual phase change function for enhanced all-weather atmospheric water harvesting ,’ was led by Xinyao Ji, He Shan, Jiazuo Zhou and colleagues. The researchers are affiliated with Northeast Forestry University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China.The researchers started with a material that already has a useful natural architecture, i.e.,wood. Ordinary wood contains long, aligned channels that move water through the plant, but its original structure is not optimised for rapidly drawing water vapour from the air. The team chemically modified balsa wood by removing lignin and part of its hemicellulose. This opened up the structure while retaining the cellulose framework, producing what the researchers call a wood sponge. The resulting material had an open porosity of 94.60% and an average macropore diameter of 10.84 micrometres, giving water vapour more direct pathways into the material.The lower section was then loaded with lithium chloride, a hygroscopic salt that strongly attracts water molecules. In tests, the resulting material could absorb moisture across a relative-humidity range of 15% to 90%. At 15% humidity, the best-performing composition absorbed 0.59 grams of water for every gram of sorbent. As humidity increased to 90%, its water uptake rose to 3.03 grams per gram. The material also reached equilibrium within 360 minutes, addressing one of the major problems that has limited practical atmospheric water harvesters, slow moisture uptake.Capturing moisture is only half of the problem. Once water has been absorbed, the material must be heated so the trapped water can be released and collected. Relying entirely on sunlight can make this step intermittent, particularly when clouds pass overhead or after sunset. To solve that problem, the researchers added a second layer above the moisture-catching wood sponge. This section contains a phase-change-material-based photothermal hydrogel that converts sunlight into heat and stores some of that energy as latent heat.The stored heat can then be released gradually, allowing water desorption to continue under weak sunlight and even in darkness. According to the study, the PCM hydrogel had a heat-storage enthalpy of 155.51 joules per gram and a solar-to-thermal energy-conversion efficiency of 90.80%. The result was a hybrid device in which the two layers perform different jobs. The wood sponge and lithium chloride concentrate on pulling moisture from the atmosphere, while the upper layer manages the energy needed to turn that captured moisture back into liquid water.This dual approach is central to the study by Ji, Shan, Zhou and their colleagues because atmospheric water harvesting is not simply a question of finding a material that can absorb lots of water. The material also has to absorb and release it quickly enough, repeatedly and with an energy input that makes sense outside a laboratory.The researchers tested the technology outdoors rather than relying solely on controlled humidity chambers. Large-scale arrays were demonstrated in Harbin and Xiamen, representing different climatic conditions and seasons. In a one-day outdoor experiment in Harbin, the system produced 1.72 litres of freshwater per kilogram of sorbent. The test was conducted during summer, when the average temperature was 29.24°C and average relative humidity was 62.95%, and the system completed four sorption-desorption cycles.The collected water was also analysed for metals and was reported by the researchers to meet World Health Organisation drinking-water standards for the parameters tested. The performance was not limited to that single test. In Xiamen, the system produced 1.37 litres per kilogram on the first outdoor day, followed by 0.96, 1.07 and 1.18 litres per kilogram on the next three days. Across longer outdoor experiments, the PHW array achieved an average production of 1.26 litres per kilogram per day.The researchers also modelled how the system could perform under different climates. Their calculations suggested that many regions could produce roughly 0.65 to 1.50 litres per kilogram per day, although output varied considerably with humidity, temperature and available sunlight. Humid regions such as Malaysia were estimated to exceed 1.6 litres per kilogram per day, while the estimate for Saudi Arabia was around 0.30 litres per kilogram per day.The work brings together expertise in wood materials and atmospheric water harvesting. Most of the researchers, including Xinyao Ji, Jiazuo Zhou, Chengyu Wang and Haiyue Yang, are affiliated with the Key Laboratory of Bio-Based Material Science and Technology of the Ministry of Education at Northeast Forestry University in Harbin. He Shan and senior researcher Ruzhu Wang are affiliated with the Engineering Research Centre of Solar Power and Refrigeration at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The choice of wood is significant because the researchers argue that it provides several advantages over more complex synthetic sorbents. Wood is naturally abundant and renewable, while its cellular structure can be modified without constructing an entirely artificial network from scratch.The study, therefore, focuses not only on increasing water uptake but on making the complete process more continuous. The authors combined rapid vapour transport, hygroscopic salt, solar heating and thermal storage into one system. The technology is not yet a replacement for conventional water infrastructure, and its output depends heavily on local weather conditions. The researchers' own global assessment found that extremely arid environments can deliver substantially less water because there is simply less atmospheric moisture available to capture.Still, the experiment demonstrates how an ordinary biological material can be redesigned into a sophisticated water-harvesting system. Instead of waiting for clouds, rain or groundwater, the device draws from a resource that is already suspended invisibly above the ground, and the researchers showed that even air with just 15% relative humidity can contain enough moisture for a carefully engineered wood sponge to collect.
Article Summary: Northeast Forestry University researchers designed the sponge for all-weather water harvesting. The technology combines a porous sponge made from balsa wood with lithium chloride, a moisture-attracting salt, and a separate layer designed to capture and store solar heat. The wood-based system produced up to 1.72 litres of water per kg.

Article Title: Priscilla Chan helped protect a Hawaiian beach preserve and wetland habitat; 17 acres are now protected for the public
Article Text:
How Priscilla Chan helped secure Kāhili Beach’s future

How the original beach parcel was protected

How the preserve expanded to 17 acres

Why the coastline and stream habitat are important

How the community is helping care for the preserve

A 17-acre stretch of coastline on Kauaʻi’s North Shore is now protected for public access and long-term conservation, with philanthropic support from Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg helping fund its ongoing stewardship. Kāhili Beach Preserve, also known locally as Rock Quarry, includes a windswept beach, the mouth of Kīlauea Stream and important riparian areas. The Hawaiʻi Land Trust owns the preserve and holds it in perpetuity. Chan and Zuckerberg did not acquire the property themselves. Instead, their endowed gift through the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund of the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation supports the long-term care of land that was first protected through a private donation in 2003 and later expanded by HILT. The preserve now combines public beach access, habitat protection, restoration and community stewardship.Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg contributed to Kāhili Beach Preserve through an endowed gift made through the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund of the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation. The Hawaiʻi Land Trust says the fund supports the preserve’s ongoing stewardship and helped establish funding for a part-time staff presence dedicated to caring for Kāhili. The contribution came after the land had already begun its conservation journey, so Chan and Zuckerberg were not the original purchasers or donors of the property.HILT’s own material says the original preserve had been protected without a dedicated stewardship fund, making long-term financial support important for its continued care. The specific value of Chan and Zuckerberg’s Kāhili gift has not been publicly disclosed in the sources available from HILT and the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation. Their contribution therefore represents support for maintaining protected land rather than the purchase of the 17-acre preserve itself.The conservation story began in November 2003, when Louise and Monte Zweben donated a 5.43-acre oceanfront parcel to the Hawaiʻi Land Trust. The property lies at the mouth of Kīlauea Stream and beside the Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge. The donation protected the shoreline while preserving public access to Kāhili Beach. The beach is also known locally as Rock Quarry and has long been used for surfing and recreation. HILT identifies public access and habitat restoration among the preserve’s main conservation values. The original donation established the foundation for protecting the coastline from future development while allowing the community to continue using the beach.The protected area grew significantly a decade later. In 2013, Hawaiʻi Land Trust purchased an adjoining 12.2-acre parcel, bringing the combined Kāhili Beach Preserve to 17.63 acres. The larger property includes the Kīlauea Stream river mouth and riparian buffer areas as well as the beach and coastal landscape. HILT owns the preserve and holds it for conservation in perpetuity. The organisation's approach means the land is not simply protected temporarily but is intended to remain conserved for future generations. The expansion also increased the amount of coastal and streamside habitat that could be managed as a connected landscape rather than as a single narrow strip of beach.Kāhili contains several interconnected coastal environments, including sandy shoreline, dunes, the Kīlauea Stream mouth and riparian habitat. HILT highlights the importance of the area's muliwai, where freshwater from the stream meets the ocean. These transition zones can provide important habitat and feeding opportunities for coastal wildlife. The preserve also supports native coastal vegetation, while the nearby Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge adds another layer of protected habitat to the surrounding landscape. HILT's conservation work at Kāhili includes addressing invasive plants, marine debris and erosion. Protecting the land therefore helps preserve more than recreational beach access. It also maintains a section of the coastal ecosystem where freshwater, terrestrial and marine environments meet.Kāhili’s conservation story has continued through local volunteer work and restoration. After the original 2003 donation, Hawaiʻi Land Trust worked with the Kīlauea Neighborhood Association on regular beach clean-ups. HILT says volunteers have contributed more than 1,000 person-hours to such efforts. More recent activities have included removing invasive vegetation and planting native coastal species. The trust also organises educational programmes and guided Talk Story on the Land experiences, giving visitors an opportunity to learn about the area's native plants, wildlife and cultural history. Together, land protection, philanthropic stewardship and community involvement have helped turn Kāhili into more than a protected parcel. The 17.63-acre preserve now provides public access while giving a coastal ecosystem a long-term layer of protection.
Article Summary: Kāhili Beach Preserve includes a windswept beach, the mouth of Kīlauea Stream and important riparian areas. Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg contributed to the preserve through an endowed gift made through the Chan Zuckerberg Kaua'i Community Fund of the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation. The original donation established the foundation for protecting the coastline from future development while allowing the community to continue using the beach.

Article Title: 'Everyone's been bugging me': Trump to remove 10% duty on Irish whiskey
Article Text:
Trump also claimed that Lowry was among those who had raised the issue with him adding that Martin and several golfers had urged him to reconsider the tariff.

US President Donald Trump attended the Irish Open in Ireland on Sunday and announced plans to remove the United States’ 10% tariff on Irish whiskey, saying he had faced repeated calls to drop the duty from Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, golfers and others.Trump made the announcement during the trophy ceremony after Irish golfer Shane Lowry won the tournament. The surprise move drew loud whistles and cheers from spectators, although it was not immediately clear when the tariff would be lifted."Everybody's been bugging me" to do it, Trump said. "And I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off" of Irish whiskey.Trump said Martin and several golfers had raised the issue with him, with Lowry among those who asked him to reconsider the tariff.Irish whiskey currently faces the standard tariff imposed by the Trump administration on most imports from the European Union. The rate was reduced from 15% to 10% in July.The planned move would also address an imbalance created after Trump announced in April that certain tariffs on whiskey from the United Kingdom would be lifted. The concession covers Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland, leaving Irish whiskey subject to a higher trade barrier.Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, welcomed Trump's announcement, calling it "another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade".He said the move would benefit businesses and consumers during the upcoming holiday season."As US hospitality businesses enter the critical holiday season, this action will provide a welcome boost for retailers, restaurants, consumers and the American economy," Swonger said.The Irish Whiskey Association had called for the tariff to be removed in May. It said doing so would help US companies that sell Irish products and reduce uncertainty for consumers.Trump had previously linked the UK tariff concession to a visit by King Charles III and Queen Camilla to the White House on April 30."The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!" Trump posted on social media at the time.The Scotch Whisky Association said on July 24 that the zero-tariff arrangement for Scotch had come into effect.
Article Summary: Irish whiskey currently faces the standard tariff imposed by the Trump administration on most imports from the European Union. The rate was reduced from 15% to 10% in July. The planned move would also address an imbalance created after Trump announced in April that certain tariffs on whiskey from the United Kingdom would be lifted.

Article Title: Russia offers Rs 16 lakh per foreign soldier for Ukraine war: Report
Article Text:
The increase in Irkutsk comes as Russian regions step up recruitment incentives amid Moscow's continuing need for manpower in its war against Ukraine

Russia turns to foreign recruits

Russia’s Irkutsk region has sharply increased financial incentives for recruiting foreign nationals into the country’s military, offering up to 1.5 million rubles (around Rs 16 lakh) for each foreign citizen or stateless person recruited to fight in the war against Ukraine.According to The Kyiv Independent, which cited independent Russian outlet Vyorstka, the new payment was established in a decree signed earlier this week by Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev. The payment is reportedly the highest reward offered by any Russian region for recruiting foreign nationals into the military.Irkutsk has offered financial incentives for recruiting contract soldiers since at least April. Previously, recruiters could receive up to 400,000 rubles (around $4,700). The latest increase means the maximum payment for recruiting a foreign national has risen almost fourfold in seven months, Vyorstka reported.The new decree also creates a separate category for foreign nationals and stateless people for the first time. Meanwhile, the payment for recruiting Russian citizens who are registered outside Irkutsk Oblast has been doubled from 400,000 rubles to 800,000 rubles (around $9,500).The increase in Irkutsk comes as Russian regions step up recruitment incentives amid Moscow's continuing need for manpower in its war against Ukraine.Other regions have also raised payments for those helping recruit soldiers. Smolensk Oblast increased its recruiter payment from 115,000 rubles (around $1,300) to 1 million rubles (around $11,900), while Ryazan Oblast has raised some recruitment payments to 805,000 rubles (around $9,500).The growing incentives also come amid increasing evidence that Russia has sought to bolster its military ranks with foreign nationals, particularly people from lower-income countries.The recruitment drive comes as fighting between Russia and Ukraine continues to intensify. Russia has stepped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones being used in attacks across the country. Ukrainian officials have also reported Russian strikes near the border with Poland.At the same time, Ukraine has continued targeting Russian oil and industrial infrastructure with long-range strikes. US President Donald Trump has called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop attacks on Russian diesel facilities, saying they were contributing to a global fuel shortage.The developments come as both sides continue to suffer casualties and infrastructure losses, while Moscow seeks additional manpower for its more than four-year-old invasion of Ukraine.
Article Summary: Irkutsk has offered financial incentives for recruiting contract soldiers since April. Previously, recruiters could receive up to 400,000 rubles (around $4,700) The maximum payment for recruiting a foreign national has risen almost fourfold in seven months.

Article Title: Russia targeting EU, UK officials? Ukraine’s big claim after drone strike
Article Text:
The drone struck a locomotive at Yahodyn station

A Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border may have been aimed at a diplomatic train carrying former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson , former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and European security officials, Ukraine’s state railway operator has claimed.The drone struck a locomotive at Yahodyn station, around 2 km from the Polish border, shortly after the diplomatic train carrying the senior officials had passed through the area. No casualties were reported.According to Ukrzaliznytsia, the diplomatic train had left the station earlier than scheduled after railway authorities adjusted timetables in real time because of the continuing threat of Russian strikes.“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train,” the railway operator said, according to the Daily Mail.Ukrzaliznytsia later confirmed that the diplomatic train had been at the site shortly before the strike. It said the train was carrying security advisers from several European Union member states, along with former European leaders including Johnson.The delegation had been returning from the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv.Bildt later shared footage of the attack on X, saying the train struck was not theirs but had been travelling just minutes behind them.“This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing,” Bildt said. “It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was hurt.”Another train carrying former CIA Director David Petraeus was reportedly still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck.Johnson condemned the attack, describing it as “random and senseless” and saying it reflected the kind of attacks Ukrainians face on a daily basis.The incident has raised concerns over the safety of foreign officials travelling through western Ukraine, particularly as the strike occurred close to the border of NATO member Poland.Russia has not said that the diplomatic train was the intended target. Moscow said its forces had targeted infrastructure facilitating the movement of military cargo from Europe into western Ukraine.The strike came amid a broader escalation in long-range attacks. Earlier on Sunday, a Russian drone also hit a truck near the Ukraine-Poland border, temporarily disrupting operations at the Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing.
Article Summary: The drone struck a locomotive at Yahodyn station, around 2 km from the Polish border, shortly after the diplomatic train carrying senior officials had passed through the area. No casualties were reported. The train was carrying security advisers from several European Union member states, along with former European leaders including Johnson.

Article Title: In the late 20th century, American soybean seeds arrived in China to increase yields, but contaminated shipments introduced invasive weeds that spread across thousands of fields
Article Text:
Soybean / Palmer amaranth | Wikimedia Commons

Amaranthus palmeri

Soybean / Palmer amaranth | Wikimedia Commons

The pathway ran through imported grain

Palmer amaranth spread beyond its first arrival points

Amaranthus palmeri

Different varieties of soybeans being grown together | Wikimedia Commons

Biosecurity became part of the soybean trade

A. palmeri

Soybean imports from the United States have carried seeds of foreign plants into Chinese ports, with some of those weeds later establishing populations beyond the places where they were first detected. One of the clearest examples is Palmer amaranth (), a weed that is native to the Americas and has become an agricultural problem in parts of China. A 2026 study in the Journal of Integrative Agriculture traced populations of the weed in China and found evidence that linked repeated introductions to imported soybean shipments.The research identified 1985 as the date of an initial introduction in Beijing and found that later populations were associated with the movement of imported soybeans. The researchers concluded that repeated introductions through global grain trade played a major role in the weed's distribution across China.Weed seeds can become mixed with harvested grain as crops are collected, stored and transported, and some seeds can survive the journey and enter agricultural areas if they are not detected or removed. Chinese officials raised concerns about this pathway directly with U.S.authorities in 2017, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said China had notified the agency about increased detections of weed seeds of quarantine concern in U.S. soybean shipments. USDA subsequently developed a farm-to-export systems approach that was intended to reduce the amount of foreign material and weed seed entering soybean consignments, which was scheduled to begin with the 2018 crop year.The issue was important enough to affect the phytosanitary conditions under which U.S. soybeans could enter the Chinese market. USDA said the measures were designed to reduce plant-pest risk while keeping soybean exports moving. A 2025 study published through the National Library of Medicine reported thatseeds had been repeatedly introduced into China as contaminants in soybean imports since 1985. The researchers found that populations were concentrated near grain-import facilities and documented cases in southern, central, northern and northeastern China.Grain facilities provide a starting point, after which seeds can move through agricultural machinery, transportation networks and crop production areas. The researchers also found that populations differed in their degree of establishment; some remained temporary, while others became naturalized or invasive and spread beyond their initial locations.Palmer amaranth is particularly difficult to manage because individual plants can produce large quantities of seed and the weed can compete aggressively with crops. Its presence in China therefore became more than a matter of contaminated cargo, and it eventually became a question of whether a plant introduced through international trade could establish itself in agricultural landscapes.Soybeans are traded in bulk, and separating every foreign seed from a large shipment is difficult, so prevention has to begin before the grain reaches a port. USDA's 2018 systems approach included measures at farms, export facilities and other points in the supply chain, with the goal being to reduce the number of weed seeds entering them in the first place.The practical problem is that once a species establishes itself in a new agricultural region, removing it can be much harder than preventing the original introduction. The newer research onsuggests that the trade route remains important, as its analysis found genetic and geographic patterns that were consistent with repeated introductions linked to soybean imports, rather than a single introduction followed by uninterrupted expansion.The original soybean shipments were part of a much larger trade system moving food and animal feed across continents, but within those cargoes, tiny quantities of weed seed could travel the same routes. In China's fields, some of those seeds found conditions in which they could establish and spread.
Article Summary: Weed seeds can become mixed with harvested grain as crops are collected, stored and transported. Some seeds can survive the journey and enter agricultural areas if they are not detected or removed. Palmer amaranth is particularly difficult to manage because individual plants can produce large quantities of seed.

Article Title: Meet Ava Grace Cummings, the 18-year-old North Carolina student who modelled STAC3 disorder, a rare hereditary muscle disease first identified in the Lumbee Tribe, in fruit flies and won $175,000 from
Article Text:
Portrait of Ava Grace Cummings along with the image of a common fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster). Credits - Instagram/lumbeetribencgov, Wikimedia Commons

A sickness deeply ingrained in her own culture

Turning fruit flies into a model of disease in action

A Drosophila melanogaster specimen is being observed under a light microscope. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Connecting Two Medical Systems

The Regeneron Science Talent Search is described by the Society for Science as the nation's oldest and most prestigious science and maths competition for high school seniors. It makes sense that most projects address issues that are somewhat unrelated to the researcher's personal life. Ava Grace Cummings made the opposite decision. The senior from Smithfield, North Carolina, who is eighteen years old, based her research on an illness she had personally witnessed in the faces of people she knew.Cummings, a member of the Lumbee and Coharie tribes, won second place and $175,000 in the 2025 competition for a study that used laboratory fruit flies to model STAC3 disorder, a rare genetic muscular condition. The flies were then used to test alternative therapies, including one based on traditional Indigenous herbal medicine.Formerly known as Native American myopathy, STAC3 disorder is a congenital ailment that lowers muscle tone from birth and can cause joint stiffness, a cleft palate, a bent spine, and a potentially fatal reaction to some anaesthetic medications. It was initially identified in babies from the Lumbee tribe of North Carolina in the late 1980s, and it was subsequently linked to a single genetic mutation that was inherited among the group.GeneReviews estimates that STAC3 disorder affects about one in 5,000 Lumbee Native Americans. The condition has also been identified in other populations, including patients in southern Africa.For Cummings, STAC3 disorder was never an abstract condition. She told the Society for Science that seeing friends and family in the Lumbee Tribe struggle with the disease motivated her to raise awareness and look for potential treatments. There is no cure for STAC3 disorder, making the search for possible therapies an important part of her project.To study the rare muscle condition without human patients, Cummings turned to Drosophila. The fruit fly is widely used in genetics research because its short life cycle makes it possible to alter genes and observe changes over a relatively short period. Cummings created a strain of flies that did not express the dstac gene, the fly counterpart of the gene disrupted in STAC3 disorder. The resulting flies showed muscle-weakness traits that allowed her to model the condition in the laboratory.Armed with a workable model, she investigated two prospective therapies. One was Tirasemtiv, an experimental drug being studied for its effects on muscle contraction and neuromuscular function. The other was stinging nettle, Urtica dioica, a plant that many traditional herbal medicines employed, some of which her tribe used. She tested affected adult flies by measuring how well they climbed the walls of a test vial, while the larvae were assessed by the distance they travelled. Flies treated with nettle extract alone climbed better, while the larvae also travelled farther than untreated groups. The combination of nettle extract and Tirasemtiv produced the strongest improvement among the treatments tested.Rather than seeing Indigenous medicine and pharmaceutical research as two separate worlds, Cummings considers her study an attempt to bring the two into parity. She has said she hopes her study will bring greater attention, funding and therapeutic interest to illnesses that impact small, unique populations and are otherwise easily overlooked by the broader medical research system.During high school, she attended the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics in Durham, where she founded and led the school's Natives Rising chapter. She also plays the piano, is a member of her school soccer team and serves as a resident life advisor. Cummings' second-place finish was also part of a notable milestone for the competition. Alongside fourth-place winner Logan Lee, a Native Hawaiian student, she was one of two Indigenous students to receive a top-10 prize in the 2025 Regeneron Science Talent Search. Native America Calling reported that it was the first time two Indigenous students had received top-10 awards in the competition's 83-year history.
Article Summary: Ava Grace Cummings won second place and $175,000 in the 2025 Regeneron Science Talent Search. She used laboratory fruit flies to model STAC3 disorder, a rare genetic muscular condition. The flies were then used to test alternative therapies, including one based on traditional Indigenous herbal medicine.

Article Title: In 2025, Skagit County bought development rights on four Washington farms totalling 270 acres, permanently protecting prime soil as housing pressure grows
Article Text:
Farm in Skagit County near Bow, Washington, U.S. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Exchanging a promise for a reward

Four families, four causes

Farmland in Skagit County. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Racing against a statewide trend

Land on the outskirts of expanding towns and communities in the United States is constantly under pressure to change from being agricultural. The soil quality that took centuries to develop is permanently lost if a field is paved over for a warehouse or divided for homes. The agriculture corridor along Interstate 5 in northwest Washington, where some of the nation's most productive soil is located within commuting distance of Seattle, is one of the few locations that best exemplifies the conflict between growth and food production. For almost thirty years, one county in that corridor has discreetly bought its way out of that pattern, one farm at a time.In 2025, Skagit County's Farmland Legacy Program protected four properties in Bow and Mount Vernon, adding 270 acres of prime farmland to the land permanently protected from residential development. The properties covered 40 and 83 acres in Bow and 40 and 107 acres in Mount Vernon, and all were designated by the US Department of Agriculture as prime farmland. A total of 585,000 dollars was paid to the four families involved under the scheme in return for giving up the right to ever build dwellings on the site.The agreement is made through what's called a conservation easement. Rather than purchasing the land, the county pays farmers for the development rights associated with it. This legal action permanently limits the site to agriculture, regardless of future ownership.Families can still farm their land, sell it or pass it on, but the easement runs with the property forever, eliminating the possibility to cash out to a housing developer. The scheme, which began in 1997, has already conserved about 15,400 acres of Skagit agriculture.The 2025 additions were from the Roozen, Nelson, Peth and Houser families, each with a long history of farming in the region. Jerry Nelson, a third-generation Skagit farmer and proprietor of Double N Potatoes, placed an easement on 40 acres near the Skagit Regional Airport. Including land protected through earlier easements, the Nelson family has now placed about 1,500 acres of Skagit farmland under the program, the most of any participant. Nelson said the relinquishment of development rights helps offset the cost of holding the site and is a basic choice not to see the area developed. He also said that dwellings across farmland made the remaining fields tougher to reach, since heavy machinery and irrigation systems did not work well alongside residential properties.The Houser family, which has farmed in the Sedro-Woolley area for generations, placed a conservation easement on 107 acres near the intersection of McLean and LaConner Whitney roads, while father-son pair Dan and Owen Peth protected more than 80 acres of their cattle ranch. Each family sacrificed a significant amount of money they could have made by selling to a developer, choosing continuity on the land over greater payment.Skagit's approach stands out because it runs directly against the wider pattern across Washington. American Farmland Trust's Farms Under Threat analysis found that Washington lost nearly 98,000 acres of farmland between 2001 and 2019, while the state's 2022 Census of Agriculture recorded a 5.2% decline in farmland. The group figures that somewhere in the country, people are converting about 2,000 acres of farmland to urban or low-density residential usage every single day, nationally.Skagit County's 2025 result came below its longer-term target of protecting an average of 400 acres a year for the next 25 years. The county had protected 460 acres in 2024, compared with 270 acres in 2025, but the annual figures are only part of a broader effort that has now placed about 15,400 acres under permanent protection. The program works through voluntary conservation easements, meaning landowners choose to give up development rights while retaining ownership and continuing to farm the property. The program's continued expansion depended not only on county funding and long-term targets but also on farmers choosing to preserve their land rather than sell its development rights.
Article Summary: Skagit County's Farmland Legacy Program protected four properties in Bow and Mount Vernon, adding 270 acres of prime farmland to the land permanently protected from residential development. The agreement is made through what's called a conservation easement. Rather than purchasing the land, the county pays farmers for the development rights associated with it. This legal action permanently limits the site to agriculture, regardless of future ownership.

Article Title: In 2023, a California materials scientist built a device that pulled drinking water from desert air; it produced 35 litres a day at just 20% humidity
Article Text:
AI Representation: A device collects drinking water from dry desert air and fills a reservoir with fresh water. Image credits: Chatgpt

The harvester ran on ambient sunlight alone

How the output shifted with humidity

An earlier MOF proved the concept could work at 20 percent humidity

Why dry air poses the harder engineering challenge

From a two-hand prototype toward household-scale units

In the summer of 2023, scientists from UC Berkeley took a machine that could be held by two hands to Death Valley National Park in North America, which is one of the most arid and hot locations on the continent and allowed it to operate using only the energy of the sun. It pulled water vapor out of the desert air, converted it to liquid and produced drinkable water without a battery, a plug, or any moving parts drawing outside power. The chemist behind the work, Omar Yaghi, had spent years building toward that single field test.This device uses a MOF, or metal-organic framework, an ultra-porous crystalline structure that Yaghi's team has studied for years. The specific MOF used here is MOF-303, an aluminum MOF that captures water molecules from the air at night, when humidity is usually higher in the desert and releases them during the day as sunlight warms the material. The resulting vapor condenses on a cooler surface within the device and flows into a container.Testing the same device in two very different climates allowed the team to isolate the effect of humidity.In Death Valley, the harvester achieved up to 210 grams of water per kilogram of MOF-303 per day in a single day-and-night cycle, marking the highest output the team recorded at that site. By comparison, in the milder, more humid air of Berkeley, the same device reached up to 285 grams per kilogram per day under similar passive operation, though Berkeley's daily averages ran lower on some days. The results appear in a 2023 paper in Nature Water , MOF water harvester produces water from Death Valley desert air in ambient sunlight, by Woochul Song, Zhiling Zheng, Ali Alawadhi and Yaghi, and they mark roughly double what an earlier passive version of the harvester had managed.Death Valley’s new technology is a further development of the tests done on the material by Yaghi and his team six years back, in collaboration with mechanical engineers from MIT. This project, which was done in 2017, involved a totally new material made up of zirconium and referred to as MOF-801. The results proved that even at low humidity levels between 20% and 30%, a solar-driven water harvester could generate significant quantities of water.The findings, published in Science as Water harvesting from air with metal-organic frameworks powered by natural sunlight, reported a yield of about 2.8 liters of water per kilogram of MOF per day at relative humidity as low as 20 percent, using only sunlight to drive the release step; some press accounts described the same result as roughly 2.8 liters over a 12-hour test window, though the paper itself reports it as a daily figure. The 2023 Nature Water study notes that switching from zirconium-based MOF-801, priced at $160 per kilogram, to aluminum-based MOF-303, priced at $3 per kilogram, made the harvester far cheaper to build; the higher water yield came from MOF-303's own adsorption behavior, not from its lower price.Water extraction from moist air is fairly easy since most dehumidifiers function on the principle of cooling air below its dew point. Nevertheless, air in the desert presents a different challenge. This is because at relative humidity less than 20%, the dew point may be below the freezing point, meaning that a lot of energy will be required for the process of condensation. MOFs are designed such that their pores are capable of adsorbing water molecules, even at very low levels of humidity, while heat can desorb them.The Death Valley test was, by design, a proof‑of‑concept prototype rather than a final, household‑scale product. The scientists pointed out that the tiny size and limited daily amount of water provided by the device were more appropriate for proving the concept behind the chemical reaction rather than for providing enough drinking water for a family's daily needs. Yaghi also disclosed in a public interview that further development along the same lines of MOF chemistry greatly enhanced production, and his firm began manufacturing more efficient devices capable of producing water in quantities of dozens or even hundreds of liters each day.
Article Summary: Device uses a MOF, or metal-organic framework, an ultra-porous crystalline structure that Yaghi's team has studied for years. The specific MOF used is MOF-303, an aluminum MOF that captures water molecules from the air at night and releases them during the day as sunlight warms the material. The resulting vapor condenses on a cooler surface within the device and flows into a container.

Article Title: In 1985, Andy Warhol created digital art on an Amiga computer; nearly 30 years later, researchers recovered 28 never-before-seen images from his floppy disks
Article Text:
Warhol used the Amiga to explore how his familiar artistic style could work in a new digital medium.

How the forgotten files were recovered

The recovered works show Warhol using digital tools to recreate subjects that were already strongly associated with his art.

Warhol’s experiments with a new medium

In 1985, Andy Warhol experimented with digital art on an Amiga computer as part of a commission from Commodore International. Nearly 30 years later, researchers recovered 28 previously unseen digital images created by the artist from floppy disks stored in the archives of The Andy Warhol Museum.The images had remained inaccessible because the files were saved in an obsolete format, according to The Andy Warhol Museum. Members of the Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) Computer Club worked with museum staff, artists and researchers to recover the data from the ageing floppy disks.Warhol, who earned a bachelor’s degree in fine arts from Carnegie Mellon University in 1949, used the Amiga to explore how his familiar artistic style could work in a new digital medium. The recovered works include experiments with Campbell’s soup cans, Botticelli’s Venus, Marilyn Monroe, a banana and portraits.The recovery project began after artist Cory Arcangel, who described himself as a "Warhol fanatic and lifelong computer nerd", learnt about Warhol’s Amiga experiments through a 1985 Commodore infomercial available on YouTube. His interest eventually led to a collaboration involving The Andy Warhol Museum, Carnegie Museum of Art, Carnegie Mellon University and the CMU Computer Club.Arcangel first approached The Andy Warhol Museum in 2011 about restoring the Amiga hardware held by the museum and checking whether files could still be recovered from its associated disks. He later worked with Tina Kukielski of the Carnegie Museum of Art, who helped connect the project with Golan Levin, a CMU art professor and director of the Frank-Ratchye STUDIO for Creative Inquiry.Levin connected Arcangel with the CMU Computer Club, a student group known for its work with obsolete computer hardware and "retrocomputing". The group found that even reading the old floppy disks could put their contents at risk. The recovery therefore required unusual equipment and methods.By February 2013, the Computer Club had prepared a plan for handling the fragile disks. Members then worked with Amber Morgan, collections manager at The Andy Warhol Museum, and other archivists to try to extract the data.At first, there was no certainty that Warhol’s artwork was still present on the disks. Many of the floppy disks were system and application disks. However, the researchers discovered that Warhol had also saved his own data on them.The directory listings provided the first major clue. Files with names such as "campbells.pic" and "marilyn1.pic" suggested that images might still exist. But the excitement quickly turned into a technical problem because the files were stored in a format that available utilities could not recognise.The Computer Club’s forensics experts eventually reverse-engineered the unknown format. This allowed them to access 28 digital images that had never been seen before. Experts at The Andy Warhol Museum judged the images to be in Warhol’s style. At least 11 of the recovered images also carried Warhol’s signature.The recovered works show Warhol using digital tools to recreate subjects that were already strongly associated with his art. Campbell’s soup cans, Venus and self-portraits appear among the images.Instead of traditional painting or printing methods, the works use digital processes available through the Amiga. These include pattern flood fills, palletised colour and copy-and-paste collage.The museum said Warhol’s Amiga experiments ranged from simple doodles and photographs of a desktop to digital versions of his familiar subjects. One work from the series, a portrait of Debbie Harry, was already part of The Warhol’s collection.Cory Arcangel said, "What's amazing is that by looking at these images, we can see how quickly Warhol seemed to intuit the essence of what it meant to express oneself.
Article Summary: Andy Warhol experimented with digital art on an Amiga computer in 1985. Nearly 30 years later, researchers recovered 28 previously unseen digital images created by the artist from floppy disks stored in the archives of The Andy Warhol Museum. The recovered works show Warhol using digital tools to recreate subjects that were already strongly associated with his art.

Article Title: In 1986, someone bought Super Mario Bros. as a Christmas gift and left it sealed in a desk drawer; 35 years later, the forgotten game sold for $660,000
Article Text:
Heritage Auctions said the copy was a pristine example of a particular Super Mario Bros. variant that was produced for an extraordinarily short period.

A short production run made it rare

A copy of Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. bought as a Christmas gift in late 1986 was placed inside a desk drawer and forgotten for 35 years. It remained sealed and untouched until it was discovered in 2021. On April 2 that year, the game sold for $660,000 at Heritage Auctions, setting a new record for the most ever paid for a video game.The game was sold as part of Heritage Auctions' Comics & Comic Art Auction in Dallas, Texas. The auction house described it as the finest known copy of the oldest sealed hangtab version of Super Mario Bros. to have been professionally graded for auction. The copy carried a Wata 9.6 A+ grade and was still sealed in its original packaging.The sale broke the previous record of $114,000, which had been set by another copy of Super Mario Bros. at a Heritage Auctions sale in July 2020. The 2021 copy was especially valuable because of its rare packaging variation and its condition.Someone bought the game in late 1986 as a Christmas gift. Instead of being opened, it was put into the bottom of an office desk drawer. It stayed there for decades without the owner realising that the unopened game could one day become a highly valuable collector's item.“It stayed in the bottom of my office desk this whole time since the day I bought it,” said the seller, who asked not to be identified. “I never thought anything about it,” he said as quoted by Heritage Auctions.The game's condition was only part of what made it special. Heritage Auctions said the copy was a pristine example of a particular Super Mario Bros. variant that was produced for an extraordinarily short period.It had a perforated cardboard hangtab and plastic shrink wrap. Heritage described it as the finest sealed copy with a perforated cardboard hangtab of any black box title it had offered. It was also the oldest factory-sealed copy of Super Mario Bros. ever offered by the auction house.The copy was produced in late 1986. According to Heritage Auctions Video Games Director Valarie McLeckie, it was among the earliest copies that came with plastic shrink wrap instead of a sticker seal.“This particular copy was produced in late 1986, and it was one of the earliest copies produced that had plastic shrink wrap, rather than sticker seal,” McLeckie said. “By early 1987, Nintendo was producing a version that had another new variation to their original packaging (an additional "code")."As soon as this copy of Super Mario Bros. arrived at Heritage, we knew the market would find it just as sensational as we did," Heritage Auctions Video Games Director Valarie McLeckie said. "Even so, the degree to which this game was embraced outside the market has been nothing short of exceptional, and that aspect of this sale has certainly exceeded our expectations. Though, I suppose we can't be too shocked; who doesn't love Mario?"
Article Summary: A copy of Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. bought as a Christmas gift in late 1986 was forgotten for 35 years. It remained sealed and untouched until it was discovered in 2021. On April 2 that year, the game sold for $660,000 at Heritage Auctions, setting a new record for the most ever paid for a video game.

Article Title: A Tennessee family wants to turn about 850 acres near the Hiwassee River into an energy campus that could host a data center; residents are raising concerns ahead of the first votes
Article Text:
Representative image

A major proposal in a rural setting

Power at the centre

Why residents are concerned

The data centre question

What supporters see

What opponents fear

The planning process

A test of transparency

What happens next

A proposed industrial campus in Bradley County, Tennessee, is putting economic development, energy demand and environmental protection on a collision course. The Wright family, owners of Wright Brothers Construction, wants to rezone and annex about 850 acres west of Interstate 75 and north of Old Lower River Road, close to the Hiwassee River. Called Project River, the development could include a power complex fuelled by natural gas and woody biomass, along with a large industrial customer such as a data center. No data center operator has signed a contract, but developers say that is the most likely use. As reported by WUTC’s Scenic Roots, the project is approaching its first planning commission and city council votes while residents continue asking questions about water, noise, traffic, emissions and the river’s future.Project River would transform land that is currently zoned for farming and agricultural use. The site is privately owned by the Wright family and lies near the Hiwassee River, a waterway important to recreation, wildlife and the identity of the surrounding community.The proposed campus has been described as an $11.3 billion investment that could create about 2,600 jobs and bring advanced industrial activity to Bradley County.Developers say the project could support energy intensive manufacturing, robotics, semiconductor production or a data center. Although the public conversation has focused heavily on artificial intelligence and data processing, the final industrial customer has not yet been selected.That uncertainty is central to the debate. Residents are being asked to consider rezoning and annexation before knowing precisely what will operate on the land. Developers have said a data center is the most likely option, but there is no confirmed operator or power customer at this stage. The project’s energy infrastructure would be built first, with the eventual customer determined later.The plan calls for up to 1,500 megawatts of on site electricity generation. That would include a 500 megawatt woody biomass plant and two natural gas plants with a combined capacity of 1,000 megawatts. A connection to the Tennessee Valley Authority grid would provide up to 360 megawatts for backup and periods of high demand.Developers describe the arrangement as a way to avoid shifting the project’s primary electricity demand onto local households and businesses. They say the campus would generate most of its own power and would not raise residents’ electricity bills.The proposed biomass facility would use pine trees and other woody material from the region. Supporters say that could revive local forestry operations and create new demand for timber suppliers, truckers and skilled workers. The natural gas plants would provide dependable energy when renewable or biomass generation could not meet the campus’s needs.Critics question whether a project that relies on large natural gas plants and extensive biomass burning should be presented as an environmentally responsible development. They are also seeking detailed information about fuel supply, emissions, ash disposal, truck traffic and the long term effects of operating such a large energy complex beside the river.At public meetings, residents have raised concerns about the scale of the proposal and the limited information available before the first votes. Water, electricity, noise and environmental impacts have been recurring topics.The Hiwassee River is central to many residents’ concerns. People use the river for boating, fishing, swimming and recreation. Businesses along its shoreline depend on visitors, while nearby landowners worry that construction and industrial operations could change the character of the area.Residents have asked whether the project could affect groundwater, erosion, wildlife habitat and river water quality. They also want to know how construction would manage stormwater and sediment, particularly on a large site near a major waterway.Developers have stated that the project would not use municipal water or draw water from the Hiwassee River for daily operations. They have also said there would be no intake or discharge pipe running into the river. Those assurances have not resolved all concerns, partly because detailed environmental and traffic studies were still pending when residents began asking questions.Data centres have become controversial across the United States because of their enormous electricity requirements, cooling systems, construction footprints and potential noise. Project River has attracted similar scrutiny even though the developers say they do not yet have a data centre contract.A data centre is the most likely customer for the proposed 1,500 megawatts, according to project leaders. The facility could support cloud computing, artificial intelligence or other high demand digital services. Such operations can bring investment and jobs, but they require reliable electricity around the clock and extensive supporting infrastructure.For residents, the uncertainty creates a trust problem. They want to know whether the community is being asked to approve a general industrial campus or a project designed primarily for a data centre. The distinction affects questions about cooling, backup generation, noise, security, water use and future expansion.Developers have said the site could also host advanced manufacturing, robotics or semiconductor production. They argue that developing the power supply first gives Bradley County flexibility to attract a range of industries rather than depending on one tenant.Supporters view Project River as a potential economic turning point. The proposal could bring billions of dollars in private investment, create construction and permanent jobs, increase the local tax base and support regional suppliers.The biomass plant could also create a new market for timber and forestry businesses. Supporters say the project could help maintain land based jobs and give local workers opportunities without requiring them to move away.Union representatives have expressed support for the project, pointing to the skilled construction and power plant jobs it could create. The economic argument is especially important in communities seeking higher paying employment and new industrial investment.Developers also say that the campus would be built in phases over about five years.
