The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (London) has been less than helpful, basically pointing the family to the Indian consulate...,”he told Parliament.The British MP also questioned why Bhattacharyya’s six decades in Britain counted for little because he had retained Indian citizenship. “He has lived in this country for 60 years. He is missing. Can we have a debate about how the FCDO can be more helpful to people who have lived in this country all their lives and are affected by such national tragedies? Because he does not have a British passport, we cannot help him.”In a subsequent social-media post, Lavery said FCDO had told the family it could not assist because Bhattacharyya held an Indian passport and had instead referred them to Indian authorities. He said he wanted a wider debate on how Britain supports long-term residents without citizenship and hoped to secure a ministerial meeting to seek answers for the family.Responding in the Commons, leader of House Alan Campbell said, “We are working with authorities on the ground to support their efforts in this terrible situation, supporting survivors of all nationalities and trying to get information for families about missing loved ones.”He added, “We are also in contact with the Indian authorities about the relief effort. I am disappointed that that has not led to the outcome that my honourable friend seeks. I will see if the relevant minister will meet with him to discuss this case and wider issues about what govts can do in what are often terrible circumstances.”Bhattacharyya was travelling with Kolkata-based Chalo Jaai Travel Club on a Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage handled in Nepal by Samrat Tours and Travels and remains among 32 members of the contingent — 30 tourists and two tour employees — who are still missing near Timure-Rasuwagadhi. Nepal immigration records showed members of the group had cleared immigration shortly before the flood struck, leaving uncertainty over whether they had crossed into Tibet or remained near the border when the torrent arrived.Bhattacharyya’s family friend has turned to Nepal’s mountaineering community for help, posting an appeal with his photograph and details of his last known movements on a forum followed by trekkers, tour operators and mountain guides.
Article Summary: Dr Anirban Bhattacharyya, 66, of Newbiggin-by-the-Sea in northeast England, remains on Nepal Police’s official missing-persons list more than two weeks after the disaster. Ashington and Blyth MP Ian Lavery alleges that authorities declined to assist in his case because he did not hold a British passport.

Article Title: Tech glitch at Adani power unit hits Bangladesh grid
Article Text:
Adani Power's 1,600 MW Jharkhand-based Godda thermal plant

DHAKA: Bangladesh's electricity supply Friday came under further strain, intensifying load shedding, after a technical "glitch" shut down one of the two units at Adani Power's 1,600 MW Jharkhand-based Godda thermal plant.The setback came amid the nation's struggle to generate enough electricity to meet demand due to shortages of coal, gas and oil, despite having 136 power plants. Several plants are regularly shut down because of fuel shortages as energy supplies from West Asia remain disrupted due to the conflict there, while others are operating below capacity.While Adani Power refused to comment, sources confirmed a "glitch" in one unit of the plant, which is likely to be repaired within 3-4 days. The problem occurred in the boiler, which may take about 48 hours to cool before repairs can begin, and as a result, it could take several days for generation to return to normal, claimed sources at Power Grid Company and Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) - which had signed a power purchase agreement with Adani Power in 2017.
Article Summary: A technical "glitch" shut down one of the two units at Adani Power's 1,600 MW Jharkhand-based Godda thermal plant. The setback came amid the nation's struggle to generate enough electricity to meet demand due to shortages of coal, gas and oil.

Article Title: US volunteers fuel Nepal relief, give 800 litres free
Article Text:
Volunteers (in red shirts) of Fuel Relief Fund (FRF) providing free fuel in flood-affected areas in Nepal.

Dehradun:

More than 800 litres of free petrol and diesel have reached hospitals, relief camps and people in flood-hit parts of Nepal through a three-member volunteer team from the US, which even used heavy-lift drones and zip-lines to move fuel into areas where roads and access routes had been washed away. The volunteers, working with the Fuel Relief Fund (FRF), have spent the past five days procuring fuel locally and distributing it according to need, while also supplying LPG cylinders to relief camps running community kitchens.Joseph Lee, a retired firefighter from Texas, and two other FRF volunteers travelled to Nepal as part of the organisation’s disaster-response effort. Lee told TOI that FRF, a volunteer-based organisation operating since 2005, had supplied fuel during nearly 30 disasters, including earthquakes in Turkey, Venezuela, Nepal and Haiti, besides emergencies in Morocco, Mozambique, the Philippines and the US. “Our organisation works purely on funds raised through donations,” he said.Lee said FRF used those donations to buy fuel from local sources in disaster-hit countries rather than transporting supplies from abroad. “We have so far distributed more than 800 litres of petrol and diesel to people and agencies in need. We understand the value of this critical resource in situations like this, and our priorities are hospitals and relief camps,” he said.Connectivity remained the biggest challenge, with several roads and approaches destroyed by the floods. “We have transported free fuel using heavy-lift drones and zip-lines where accessibility was washed away, and we also work with local associates to make sure it reaches those who actually need it,” Lee said.His co-volunteer Katherine said the team had also supplied LPG cylinders to remote relief camps after community kitchens began running short of cooking fuel. “Many community kitchens were short of cooking fuel, so we provided LPG cylinders to ensure survivors continued getting meals. We will continue despite the challenges,” she said.Lee said five more FRF volunteers would join the team in Nepal within days, expanding its relief operations. On Thursday, the group left with 210 litres of fuel for Dhunche, one of the areas badly affected by the floods, despite difficult road conditions. “Reaching there is difficult because of the poor roads, but we are determined to extend our help,” he said.Saurab Rimal, founder of Nepal-based NGO Karmayog Foundation, which is also involved in relief work, praised the initiative. “What they are doing is really appreciable in this situation. I haven’t seen anyone else doing this so far,” he said.
Article Summary: Volunteers from the US have provided more than 800 litres of free petrol and diesel to people in flood-hit parts of Nepal. The volunteers, working with the Fuel Relief Fund (FRF), have spent the past five days procuring fuel locally and distributing it according to need.
